Product requirements · v0.1 draft · Mycelium Onslaught

Mycelium
OnslaughtA total-conversion reskin of Onslaught 2

The fungi are winning. You are the fungi. The systems of the 2008 original are preserved exactly; every number is our own, generated rather than ported. What changes is who you are, what you build, and what comes down the road to stop you.

Section one

1Premise and frame

A reskin only works if the fiction explains the mechanics rather than fighting them. This one was chosen because the original's structure already tells a fungal story.

1.1The inversion

In the original you are a base defending against attackers. Here the base is a Mycelial Core — a primordial fruiting mass — and the things walking down the road are the resistance: ants first, then rodents, birds, mammals, and finally humans in hazmat and armour. You build fungal structures along the trail to stop them reaching the Core.

The player is the invasive intelligence. That is the single narrative move the whole reskin rests on, and it costs nothing mechanically: "attackers" and "base" keep their exact roles.

1.2Why the enemy ladder repeats

The original cycles nine attacker sprites with (wave − 1) % 9 while HP compounds every wave. That looks arbitrary until you give it a fiction: each pass through the nine tiers is one escalation cycle of the global response. Ants come back at wave 10 because a new colony was recruited, better fed, harder to kill. Humans come back at wave 18 with better gear.

This lets the HP curve — which reaches absurd numbers by design — read as narrative escalation instead of a number going up. Cycle number should be surfaced in the HUD (see §4.3).

1.3What must not change

The systems are locked; the constants are ours. That split is deliberate — see §5 for why, and §9 D6 for what it resolves. Locked means:

  • Colour-led combo dispatch. First tower to acquire the target runs the recipe list; counts exclude the firing tower; first match wins.
  • Additive multiplier stacking with a floor. eff = max(0, (base + Σadded) × max(0.2, 1 + Σmult)). Two +45% modifiers give ×1.90, not ×2.10.
  • Three independent upgrade tracks per tower, with combo eligibility gated on the damage track alone.
  • Endless compounding waves with a decaying growth rate, fixed wave size, and spawn spacing inside a wave.
  • Tick rates per system, fixed in milliseconds — never driven off the render loop.
  • All balance values come from balance.json, generated by generate_balance.py. No constant is ever typed into game code.

The last point is what the review gate enforces (§7.3): a commit that hard-codes a balance number, or that edits balance.json without a corresponding generator change, fails check 2 and is escalated.

Hard constraint — colour identity

The combo system dispatches on tower colour. A player reads a cluster and predicts which combo fires by counting red, green, blue and yellow caps at a glance, at 100% zoom, with thirty towers on screen. Any art direction that makes two families confusable breaks the deepest layer of the game.

Colour family assignment is therefore frozen at the design level and every asset is validated against it (§3.4). Species choice serves the colour, never the other way round.

Section two

2Asset mapping

Every entity in the original gets exactly one counterpart. Where a real fungus does the mechanical job the tower does, we use it — the game is more interesting when the biology is true.

2.1The four core families

Puffball Battery was Blue Cannon
Lycoperdon perlatum · rapid spore percussion

Cheap, fast, short-legged. Squeezes visible puffs of spore dust at the trail. Its freak-out is a chain-reaction of the whole cluster venting at once — 3× damage, 4× rate, five seconds. Silhouette: low round dome, no stalk.

Foxfire Lantern was Green Laser
Mycena chlorophos · bioluminescent beam

Emits a continuous green light beam. Links to neighbouring lanterns and relays power along the chain at ×1.25 per link — the mycelial network made literal. Silhouette: tall thin stalk, small flat glowing cap.

Artillery Cap was Red Rocket
Amanita muscaria / Sphaerobolus · ballistic spore packet

Longest range, biggest damage, priciest ladder. At range 3 / rate 3 it holds up to four spore packets in orbit, pre-launched. Silhouette: fat domed cap with high-contrast speckling, thick stalk with volva.

Cordyceps Spire was Yellow Tazer
Ophiocordyceps unilateralis · behavioural arrest

Short range, slow, and the only source of slow. Poison divides target speed by up to 10. The most on-the-nose casting in the game: cordyceps genuinely hijacks and paralyses insects. Silhouette: antler-like branching spike, no cap.

2.2Support structures

Modifiers never fire. They are underground infrastructure surfacing just enough to be seen — the mycelium, not the mushroom. Visually they should read as a distinct class at a glance: low, wide, no barrel, faint pulsing rhizomorph threads reaching toward whatever they buff.

Ghost Mycelium — an art problem worth solving

The original Combonly is literally invisible (_alpha = 0), which is unteachable. Since it is the game's precision tool, give it a build-mode-only presence: visible as a faint subterranean glow while the build panel is open or while C is held, invisible during normal play. Mechanically identical, dramatically more learnable.

2.4The enemy ladder

Nine tiers, cycling. Tier index is (wave − 1) % 9, cycle number is floor((wave − 1) / 9) + 1. The repoint flag — which decides whether a sprite rotates to face its heading — is inherited per index and should drive the rig choice: non-rotating tiers get a top-down symmetric read, rotating tiers get a clear front.

2.6The Core and the lives display

In the original the base is a green "USAF / AREA 51" sign carrying ten stick figures — that row of figures is the lives readout, and figures grey out as lives are lost. It is the best piece of design in the original UI and it must survive.

The Core becomes a swollen primordial fruiting mass. The ten figures become ten spore nodes ringing it, each lit and slowly pulsing. A breach extinguishes one node with a short dimming animation and a drop in the Core's ambient glow. At two nodes remaining the Core's pulse rate rises — a diegetic low-health warning, no HUD text needed.

Section three

3Art direction

"HD pixel, extreme colour" is a real technique with real rules, not a filter. Getting the rules explicit up front is what stops thirty separate assets drifting apart.

3.1What HD pixel means here

Pixel art at a high native resolution and full colour depth, still authored on a strict grid with hard edges. Concretely: no palette ceiling, no dithering-as-necessity, freely used gradients within a cluster — but every sprite is drawn at 1:1 on its grid, scaled only by integers, and never anti-aliased at the sprite boundary.

The failure mode to avoid is "illustration with a pixelate filter." The tell is sub-pixel detail that shimmers when the sprite moves, and edges that soften under scaling. Both are caught by the checks in §3.5.

3.2Playfield scale

The original's logical playfield is 720 × 480 with a 28 px road stroke, and all thirteen map polylines are authored in that space. Keep the logical space identical so map data ports unchanged, and render at 2× integer scale (1440 × 960) as the baseline, with 3× available for high-DPI. Sprite native sizes above are given in logical pixels — a 96 px tower occupies 96 logical px and is drawn from a 192 px source at 2×.

This is the cheapest possible route to "HD": the game keeps its exact geometry, hit tests, ranges and the 70 px combo radius, and every one of those numbers stays meaningful.

3.3Palette

Ground is dark, wet and desaturated so the towers can be loud. Forest floor in deep umber and black-green; the trail is compacted earth and rotting wood, lighter than the floor so the path reads instantly. All chroma budget goes to the fungi and their effects.

Family colour lockhue ranges are normative · shape is the second channel
FamilyHue lockSilhouette lockGlowNever
Puffballcyan–teal, 175–195°wide low dome, no stalkcool rim, low bloomany green cast
Foxfireacid green, 80–105°tall thin stalk, small capstrong emissive coreany teal cast
Artillerycrimson–magenta, 340–5°fat speckled dome + volvawarm, minimalorange drift toward amber
Cordycepsamber–gold, 38–52°branching antler, no cappulsing, slowred drift toward crimson
The two collision risks are cyan↔green and crimson↔amber. Silhouette is what saves them for colour-vision-deficient players — dome / stalk / speckled dome / antler are distinguishable in greyscale.

3.4Accessibility as a build gate

Two automated checks run on every tower asset before it can be committed:

  1. Greyscale silhouette test. Desaturate the four family sprites, downscale to 48 px, and confirm a human can name all four. Automate the proxy: pairwise silhouette IoU must be below 0.6.
  2. CVD simulation. Render the four families under deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia. No two families may fall within ΔE 2000 < 20 of each other in any simulation.

These are not polish items. They gate §2's hard constraint, so they belong in the adversarial reviewer's checklist (§7.3) rather than a QA backlog.

3.5Pixel-integrity checks

// run per sprite sheet, pre-commit 1. EDGE HARDNESS every boundary pixel is fully opaque or fully transparent (alpha ∈ {0, 255}); no partial alpha on the silhouette 2. GRID ALIGNMENT sheet dimensions divisible by the declared frame size 3. NO SUBPIXEL downscale 50%, upscale 200% nearest — diff vs original must be empty outside declared soft-glow layers 4. SCALE PARITY 2× and 3× renders are exact integer multiples; no resampling artefacts introduced 5. PALETTE DRIFT sprite mean hue sits inside the family hue lock (§3.3)

Soft glow is the one permitted exception to rule 1 and it lives on a separate additive layer, never on the sprite silhouette itself. That separation is what keeps "colourful and glowing" from becoming "blurry".

3.6Animation budget

Fungi do not move much, which is a gift. Idle animation should be breathing, not acting — a slow 4–8 frame swell at roughly 0.5 Hz, desynchronised per instance so a field of thirty towers shimmers rather than pulses in lockstep. Fire animations are short and punchy. All told the reskin needs roughly 1,100 authored frames; see §8 for how that splits across milestones.

4.3The one information gap

The original HUD shows Cash, Kills and Wave. It never shows which of the nine attacker tiers is coming, or how far into the escalation you are — a player at wave 37 has to compute (37 − 1) % 9 = 1 in their head to know beetles are next.

Given §1.2 makes the cycle narratively load-bearing, add a single line beside the run stats: Cycle n · Tier name, showing the incoming wave's tier. It is four words, it costs no layout, and it converts an invisible modulo into the game's escalation story.

Scope discipline

This is the only HUD addition sanctioned by this document. Everything else in the bar is a 1:1 reskin. If a build agent proposes further HUD changes, that is a §7 deviation and needs logging, not silent adoption.

Section five

6User research plan

The reskin carries exactly three risks worth spending research money on. Everything else is taste and can be settled by the team.

6.1Objectives and research questions

Research questions, ranked by risk
#QuestionWhy it is a riskMethod
RQ1Can players still read tower colour families at speed, under load, with the new art?Combo dispatch depends on it. If this fails the reskin has broken the game's deepest system and no amount of polish recovers it.Usability test + timed sort task
RQ2Do new players understand that they are the fungus?The premise inverts the genre's default. If it does not land in 60 seconds, the fiction is decoration rather than comprehension aid.First-session interview
RQ3Does HD pixel art at 30+ towers on screen stay legible, or turn to noise?Original assets were tiny and flat by necessity. Richer sprites at the same density may destroy the read.A/B on sprite detail level
RQ4Does the cycle indicator (§4.3) change how players plan?It is the only mechanical addition. If nobody uses it, cut it.Usability test, instrumented
RQ5Do returning Onslaught players accept the renames?A small, loyal, opinionated audience with a decade of muscle memory for "Nuke" and "BFG".Survey to TD communities

6.2Method matrix

Study plantwo participant pools · six weeks total
StudyMethodnDurationCovers
A — Colour legibilityModerated usability test with a timed identification task81 wkRQ1, RQ3
B — First sessionSemi-structured interview around a 20-minute unassisted play62 wksRQ2, RQ4
C — Sprite densityUnmoderated A/B, two detail levels, same save state at wave 40601 wkRQ3
D — Returning playersSurvey distributed to TD communities and the old forum diaspora100+2 wksRQ5
Pool 1: no prior Onslaught exposure, some tower-defence experience. Pool 2: played Onslaught 2 for 5+ hours. Studies A and C need both pools; B needs pool 1 only; D needs pool 2 only.

6.3Study A — the task that actually matters

Everything else in the research plan is conventional. This one is the reason the plan exists, so it is specified precisely.

// Timed cluster-identification task SETUP Static screenshots of the playfield at wave 40 density. Each shows one combo cluster of 3–5 towers among ~25 others. TASK "Which combo will this cluster fire?" Participant has the dispatch table on a card beside them. 12 trials, randomised, mixed difficulty. MEASURE time-to-answer, accuracy, self-reported confidence (1–5) PASS ≥ 85% accuracy AND median time-to-answer ≤ 6 s Original-art control group establishes the baseline; new art must not be more than 1.5 s slower. FAIL → art direction returns to §3.3 and the silhouette locks are tightened before any further asset work proceeds.

6.4Interview guide — Study B

50 minutes, following a standard five-part structure.

  • Warm-up (5 min). What have you played recently? What makes a tower defence good or bad for you?
  • Context (10 min). Walk me through how you normally approach a new TD game. Where do you usually get stuck? Do you read tutorials or work it out?
  • Play (20 min). Unassisted, think-aloud, no help offered. Observe silently. Note the moment — if it arrives — where they articulate what they are playing as.
  • Reaction (10 min). "Tell me the story of what just happened." Then, only if not already volunteered: "Who were you in that game?" Then show the tier ladder and ask what they expected to come next.
  • Wrap (5 min). What would you tell a friend this game is? Anything confusing we did not cover?

The one probe to avoid leading: never say "fungus" before the participant does. Time-to-first-unprompted-mention is the primary measure for RQ2.

6.5Synthesis and decision gates

Affinity-map observations across A and B; run an impact/effort matrix on everything that surfaces. Three findings are pre-committed to decisions so the research cannot be quietly ignored:

  • RQ1 fails → art direction is blocked; silhouette and hue locks are revised before any further tower assets are authored.
  • RQ2: fewer than 4 of 6 identify the inversion unprompted → add a 15-second cold open before the first wave. Not a tutorial; a single establishing beat.
  • RQ4: cycle indicator used by fewer than half → cut it and revert §4.3 to a pure 1:1 reskin.
Section six

7Build protocol

The work is wide and shallow — dozens of near-independent assets and systems against a fixed spec. That suits parallel agents. What it needs in exchange is a gate that stops drift, because thirty agents each making one small reasonable compromise produces a game that matches nothing.

7.1Roles

Agent roles
RoleOwnsMay not
OrchestratorDecomposes work, spawns implementers, sequences merges, owns the deviation logWrite production code; approve its own work
ImplementerOne work item end to end: code, assets, tests, self-check against its acceptance criteriaMerge; modify the PRD; change another item's scope
AdversaryReviews every proposed commit against this document; issues the verdictWrite the fix itself; block on taste; expand scope
ScribeAppends to DEVIATIONS.md on every forced passEdit or remove prior entries

7.2Where to fan out

Use subagents where work items are genuinely independent and have a written acceptance test. Do not fan out on the engine core — it is one coherent thing and parallelising it produces merge pain for no speed.

Decompositionparallel width per phase
WorkAgentsRationale
Engine core — tick loop, stat math, combo dispatch1Single owner. Every number is cross-coupled; parallelism here creates bugs, not throughput.
Tower assets4One agent per colour family. Family is the natural seam and the colour lock is per-family.
Enemy assets3One per size band (48 / 64 / 80 px) so rig and frame budget are shared within a band.
Modifier + apex assets2Modifiers share a visual class; apex structures share a scale.
Combo effects3Split by base sheet — sporeshell, sclerotium, bloom/miscellaneous.
UI screens2Menus and HUD are separate surfaces with no shared state.
Map + terrain rendering1Data is fixed; this is one renderer.
Audio1Coherence matters more than speed.
Peak parallel width is 8–10. Beyond that the adversary becomes the bottleneck and review quality drops, which defeats the purpose.

7.3The adversarial commit gate

No commit reaches the main branch without an adversary verdict. The adversary's job is conformance to this document, and nothing else. It reviews against a fixed checklist so its judgement is reproducible rather than moody.

// Adversary checklist — every commit, in order 1. SPEC ANCHOR Does the change cite the PRD section it implements? No citation → REVISE, immediately, without further review. 2. MECHANICS (a) Re-run generate_balance.py and diff against the committed balance.json. Any drift → fail. (b) grep the diff for hard-coded balance numbers in game code. Any hit → fail. (c) Any §1.3 locked system altered? → fail. → REVISE at attempts 1–2, then REJECT-AND-ESCALATE. Never PASS-WITH-DEBT. Outside the attempt budget. 3. ACCEPTANCE Does it satisfy every acceptance criterion on its work item? Enumerate each as met / unmet. 4. ART GATES If assets changed: run §3.4 CVD + silhouette checks and §3.5 pixel-integrity checks. Attach the output. 5. SCOPE Anything here NOT required by the cited section? Unrequested additions → REVISE. 6. REGRESSION Do existing tests pass? Was a test added for new behaviour? VERDICTS PASS all checks met — merge REVISE one or more unmet — return with specifics, decrement budget PASS-WITH-DEBT attempt budget exhausted — merge AND log (§7.5). Available for checks 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 only. REJECT-AND-ESCALATE check 2 failed at attempt 3 — does NOT merge, is NOT logged as debt, goes to a human. Terminal.

7.4Attempt budget and the forced pass

An implementer gets its initial submission plus two correction attempts. On the third submission the adversary must not issue REVISE again — it issues PASS-WITH-DEBT, the change merges, and the shortfall is written down rather than argued about.

submission 1 → PASS → merge → REVISE (budget 2 → 1) ↓ submission 2 → PASS → merge → REVISE (budget 1 → 0) ↓ submission 3 → PASS → merge → budget exhausted → PASS-WITH-DEBT → merge + DEVIATIONS.md // The adversary MAY NOT issue REVISE at submission 3. // It MAY complete trivial mechanical fixes itself at that point // (formatting, a missing test name) — and must log what it touched. // MECHANICS PATH — separate, and it never rejoins the above: check 2 fails → attempt 1 → REVISE → attempt 2 → REVISE → attempt 3 → REJECT-AND-ESCALATE → human. Stop.
Absolute — no force-pass path exists

A §1.3 mechanics violation is never force-passed, under any circumstance, at any attempt count, by any agent. If submission 3 still alters a constant, formula or dispatch condition, the item does not merge: it is rejected and escalated to a human, and the work stops there.

The adversary has no discretion here and no override. It may not accept a mechanics change as debt, may not fix it itself, and may not reclassify it as a lower-severity finding to unblock a queue. The forced pass exists to stop agents deadlocking on polish — the balance data is not polish.

7.5Deviation log

Every PASS-WITH-DEBT appends one entry to DEVIATIONS.md. The log is append-only and is reviewed by a human at each milestone boundary. Entries are never deleted; they are closed with a follow-up commit reference.

## DEV-018 · 2026-08-14 · commit a3f9c21 **Item** TOWER-ASSETS-AMBER · Cordyceps Spire idle sheet **PRD** §3.3 family colour lock, §3.5 pixel integrity **Unmet** Sprite mean hue measured 34° — outside the 38–52° amber lock. Drifts toward the crimson family under protanopia (ΔE 17.4, threshold 20). **Accepted** Merged at attempt 3. Silhouette check passes cleanly (antler form, IoU 0.31 vs nearest neighbour), so the second channel still separates it. **Fixed by adversary** Frame timing metadata corrected (8 → 6 frames declared). **Severity** MEDIUM — legibility risk, not a mechanics break **Follow-up** Re-grade the amber ramp before Study A (§6.3). OPEN.

Severity drives what happens at the milestone review:

  • LOW — cosmetic or documentation. Batch and fix opportunistically.
  • MEDIUM — affects legibility, feel or accessibility. Must be closed before the milestone that depends on it ships.
  • HIGH — affects a system another item builds on. Blocks the next milestone until closed.
  • CRITICAL — cannot occur. There is no CRITICAL row in this log by construction: a §1.3 violation is escalated and never merges, so it never becomes debt. If a CRITICAL entry ever appears, the gate itself has failed and the protocol needs auditing before work resumes.

7.6What the adversary may not do

The failure mode of an adversarial reviewer is that it becomes a second author with veto power. Explicit limits:

  • No rewriting. It reports unmet criteria; the implementer fixes them. The sole exception is the trivial-fix allowance at submission 3, which must be logged.
  • No taste vetoes. "I would have done this differently" is not a finding. Every REVISE must cite a PRD section or a failing check.
  • No scope expansion. It may not require work the cited section does not call for. If it spots genuine missing work, that becomes a new item for the orchestrator, not a condition on this commit.
  • No silent standards. If it applies a rule, the rule must be in this document. Otherwise the PRD gets amended first, by a human.

7.7Definition of done

A work item is done when: it cites its PRD section; every acceptance criterion is enumerated met; art gates pass or are logged; tests cover new behaviour; and it carries an adversary verdict of PASS or PASS-WITH-DEBT. Nothing merges on an implementer's own assessment.

Section seven

8Milestones

Sequenced so the riskiest question — RQ1, colour legibility — is answerable as early as possible, on the smallest amount of finished art.

Delivery sequence
MMilestoneContainsExit condition
M0Mechanics parityEngine core against the reference data. Original placeholder art. All 13 maps loading.A scripted 60-wave run matches reference HP, bounty and combo dispatch exactly
M1Four familiesOnly the four core tower families, fully authored. Everything else placeholder.Study A runs and passes (§6.3). This is the gate on all further art.
M2Enemy ladderAll 9 tiers, walk and death, cycle accessory overlaysTier identifiable at 48 px in greyscale by 8/8 reviewers
M3Support + apex7 modifiers, 3 supers, 2 utility, Ghost Mycelium build-mode visibilityFull 16-structure build rack playable
M4Combos20 payload effects, laser chain brightening, combo thread overlayAll 20 reachable in a sandbox harness; payload scales with cluster investment
M5Shell + CoreTitle, map select, info panel, game over, Core with 10 nodesStudy B runs (§6.4)
M6Audio + polishSound pass, deviation log burndownZero open HIGH deviations; all MEDIUM triaged
Why M0 uses the original art

Separating mechanics parity from the reskin means a failure at M0 is unambiguously an engine bug, and a failure at M1 is unambiguously an art problem. Mixing them produces the worst debugging experience available. M0 also gives Study A its control group for free — and because M0 already runs on generated balance, it doubles as the first real play-test of §5.

Section eight

9Open decisions

Things this document deliberately does not settle, flagged so they get decided rather than defaulted.

Needs a decision
#QuestionDefault if unanswered
D1Target platform and engineWeb canvas, so the original's audience can reach it as they always did
D2Do we keep the map editor and community map sharing?Ship the 13 built-ins first; editor is post-launch. Map format stays compatible regardless.
D3Does the mod system survive? Every constant is exposed as an editable value in the original.Keep the data-driven structure, defer the mod UI. The structure costs nothing and enables it later.
D4Score submission — local only, or a leaderboard?Local only at launch. Leaderboards need anti-cheat the original never had.
D5Do we publish the balance generator alongside the game?Yes. It is a genuinely interesting artefact and it makes the modding story trivial.
D6Is there any licence or attribution obligation to the original author?Largely addressed — see §5. No balance number is ported; every constant is generated from our own model. Residual questions are structural similarity and the derivative premise, which are judgement calls rather than engineering ones.
D6 — what changed and what is left

The original plan ported the reference balance tables verbatim, which was the sharpest exposure and the reason D6 blocked M0. §5 replaces that entirely: costs, ladders, wave curves and modifier values are now solved from a power model and a handful of design targets. Nothing is copied, and the generated economy is better behaved than the one it replaces on three counts.

What remains is not a data question. The game still shares its systems with the reference — colour-led combo dispatch, additive modifier stacking, endless compounding waves. Systems of play are generally a much weaker basis for a claim than copied tables, but "generally" is doing work in that sentence and I am not the right person to sign it off. Two things still worth doing: decide whether to seek the author's blessing regardless (it is one email, and the goodwill is worth more than the risk reduction), and have someone qualified look at the finished thing before it goes public.
